Ensito, with his custom-made Labubu teeth, posing with a new doll in his collection

For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.

Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more.

Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.

The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.

Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".

He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.

But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."

Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.

It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.

Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.

The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.

Pop Mart didn't invent blind boxes but its dolls certainly helped to popularise them around the world.

The sales tactic made collecting feel "nostalgic", evoking the feeling of opening gifts as a child, says marketing professional Katelynn Carlson, who discovered Labubus through social media and now owns 36 of them.

One of her first Labubus was a rare doll, making the experience "even more exciting", she adds.

Labubu, which launched in 2019, has been Pop Mart's most successful line of toys . The monsters became fashion statements and were sported by celebrities including Kim Kardashian and Blackpink's Lisa.

They regularly attracted long queues and became so popular that Pop Mart had to temporarily pull the toys from its UK shops after reports of customers fighting over them. One fan paid more than $150,000 for a human-sized Labubu .

A key part of the allure was how difficult some Labubu dolls were to find , with fans repeatedly buying blind boxes to get the version they wanted, says National University of Singapore marketing lecturer Samer El Hajjar.

Katelynn Carlson believes blind boxes were an exciting feature of the Labubu craze

Pop Mart now has more than 670 shops and at least 2,800 vending machines worldwide. The firm, which listed in Hong Kong in 2020, is worth nearly $24bn and remains one of the world's most valuable toymakers, despite its shares having fallen by more than 50% from last year's peak.

Investors worry its global success was just a viral moment rather than sustainable growth driven by long-term customer loyalty, El Hajjar says.

For Ensito, it is clear the dolls' exclusivity helped fuel the craze.

"Now it doesn't feel that way. I walk into a Pop Mart and there's a whole series of Labubus sitting there," he says.

Ashley Dudarenok of China research firm ChoZan says that sense of exclusivity faded as Pop Mart ramped up production to meet demand.

Pop Mart declined to comment on share price moves and did not respond to questions about falling sales.

As the Labubu mania cools, some of its rivals have become more popular.

Blind box collectables like Sonny Angels - tiny, unclothed cherub-like dolls - and miniature glow-in-the-dark Smiski figurines have been flying off shelves. And you can now find My Little Pony and KPop Demon Hunters in blind boxes too.

Miniso, founded in the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou, sells a range of blind-boxed Disney and Marvel characters in more than 8,000 shops globally.

"Consumers aren't particularly concerned about where the brand comes from," Miniso executive Vincent Huang said earlier this year . "They're more focused on the shopping experience - the designs, value for money, and enjoyment."

Pop Mart faces competition from retailers like Miniso

Experts say one of Pop Mart's biggest challenges is creating enduring characters.

That's an area where Hello Kitty brand Sanrio, which posted record earnings in the year to March, has a clear advantage, analyst Boustani suggests.

Pop Mart has invested heavily in ways to grow its brand, including setting up a theme park in Beijing and announcing a Labubu film - following in the footsteps of franchising giants like Disney or Lego, some experts believe.

But unlike Disney, which sells a story before it sells a toy, Pop Mart is working in reverse, says Dudarenok. "The real test for next year is whether Pop Mart can make people love a character without a celebrity holding it."

Glow-in-the-dark Smiskis are emerging as a competitor to Labubus

After spending huge sums on the monsters, collector Ensito says he is now questioning how much time and money people invest in collections each time a new trend comes along. "There's always going to be a trend every year. There's always gonna be something that's gonna be really popular."

Melbourne-based content creator Lawrence Yu says that after two years of chasing Labubus, he's likely to be "more selective" before adding to his roughly 50 dolls.

His Labubu shopping and unboxing clips once drew up to a million views but the frenzy has faded and Yu rarely makes videos about them now. "I definitely think the trend has slowed down... People go crazy and then it fizzles."

Clara Barbero from Canada believes Labubus are a "dead trend" but is still keeping an eye out for interesting releases.

"I’m curating my collection more and only buying what I see myself liking for the next few years, and not just buying the newest series that’s out."

Lawrence Yu says he has spent about $1,400 on Labubu dolls

But the fluffy monsters still have truly devoted fans.

Hedy Khaled from Liverpool says although the hype around the dolls is cooling, she is just as attached to her collection of 70 Pop Mart figurines.

There's a distinction between those who chase trends and "real fans", she argues, so falling sales do not necessarily mean Labubus have lost their appeal.

For Carlson says it is the happiness the dolls bring, not the viral trend, that keeps her collecting. She still gets excited about new Pop Mart releases, like its recent cat-themed Labubu series, which has become one of her favourites.

"I think there's something special about embracing our inner child and enjoying things simply because they make us happy."

KIGALI – Eastern, Southern and Western provinces are set to receive significantly more money from the central government than Kigali and Northern Province in the 2026/2027 financial year, raising questions about how Rwanda distributes public resources among its five administrative areas.

According to the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning’s 2026/2027 Budget Factsheet, Eastern Province has been allocated Rwf238.6 billion, followed by Southern Province with Rwf233.8 billion and Western Province with Rwf230 billion.

Northern Province, meanwhile, will receive Rwf171.2 billion, while the City of Kigali has been allocated Rwf74 billion.

The difference is particularly striking when the three leading provinces are considered together. They will receive Rwf702.4 billion, representing about 74% of the Rwf947.6 billion allocated to the five areas.

Rwanda’s total national budget for the 2026/2027 financial year stands at Rwf7,796.3 billion, up from Rwf6,952.1 billion in the revised 2025/2026 budget. The decentralized allocations account for approximately 12.2% of the national budget, with the remaining resources covering national programmes, salaries, infrastructure investments and other government expenditure.

However, the Rwf947.6 billion is not the full budget available to these regions. The figures cover transfers from the central government, including earmarked funding and block grants supporting district operations. They exclude revenues that districts and the City of Kigali generate locally and approve through their respective councils.

This distinction is important because districts have different capacities to raise their own revenue. Border districts, for example, can benefit from cross-border trade and related business activities. Others, including Muhanga, Musanze and Bugesera, have growing commercial activity, tourism, residential development and economic links with Kigali that can generate local revenue.

Consequently, a district receiving a smaller central government transfer may still have significant resources from its own economic activities. The factsheet does not provide figures showing how much each district collects locally.

Part of the explanation could lie in population distribution.

Eastern Province has approximately 3.56 million residents, making it Rwanda’s most populous province. Southern Province has about three million people, while Western Province has approximately 2.9 million.

Northern Province has around 2.04 million residents, compared with approximately 1.75 million in Kigali.

The larger populations in the Eastern, Southern and Western provinces mean greater demand for public services, including schools, health facilities, water, sanitation and agricultural support.

The number of districts could also influence the distribution. Southern Province has eight districts, Eastern and Western each have seven, Northern has five, while Kigali has three.

More districts generally mean more local administrative structures and potentially greater demand for government transfers.

The rural population is another factor worth considering.

More than three-quarters of residents in each of the four provinces live in rural areas. The proportion is particularly high in Southern Province, where about 85% of the population lives in rural communities.

In contrast, only about 13% of Kigali’s population lives in rural areas.

This difference matters because decentralized funding includes programmes such as school feeding, education capitation grants, and seed and fertiliser subsidies.

These programmes can generate substantial spending in rural areas, where agriculture and access to basic services remain important development priorities.

However, rural population alone cannot explain the differences. Northern Province is also predominantly rural, yet its total allocation is considerably lower than those of the three leading provinces.

Interestingly, looking at allocations against population produces a different picture.

When the figures are divided by the respective populations, Northern Province receives approximately Rwf84,000 per resident, compared with Rwf67,000 in Eastern Province.

Western and Southern provinces receive approximately Rwf79,000 and Rwf78,000 per resident, respectively.

Kigali receives approximately Rwf42,000 per resident.

This suggests that Northern Province’s lower overall allocation is partly explained by its smaller population. It does not necessarily mean that residents there receive less government support individually.

Bruno Fernandes' penalty sparked Manchester United's second-half revival against Roma in the Champions League

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick says captain Bruno Fernandes' commitment to the club is "undoubted" and the midfielder is "as good as ever".

Fernandes was left on the bench for October's home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick and his coaching staff in the wake of the 4-1 Champions League hammering in Como.

Restored to the team for the Premier League defeat by Chelsea a week later, Fernandes scored a retaken penalty to spark his side's stunning second-half comeback against Roma on Tuesday.

Portugal international Fernandes said afterwards there had been "a lot of lies" reported about his relationship with Carrick.

The 32-year-old rejected the notion there had been "clear-the-air talks" between the pair - something which had been confirmed by club sources.

"I think his actions, the way he's played and how he dealt with even retaking the penalty and frame of mind he was in for that, tells [you] everything," Carrick said.

A half-time speech, a retaken penalty - and a win to save Carrick's job?

Carrick refused to discuss the detail of his conversations with Fernandes following the Bournemouth loss, but says discussions are part of everyday life at Carrington.

"There are always conversations, and bits going on," he said. "It's acknowledging when things are going well and what we need to improve on.

"Sometimes it's individually, sometimes it's [a] group. What's actually said in that discussion, I'll keep that to myself, but it's pretty clear we've moved in a good direction.

"Bruno's commitment is undoubted for me in terms of what he brings to this team and this club."

It is anticipated United's powerbrokers will assess the managerial situation after Sunday's Premier League game against Aston Villa at Old Trafford.

Carrick accepts he does not know what will happen but he will be aware that only one victory in nine games – against Ipswich in August – is not good enough. The victory over Roma must be the start of a recovery.

"While we can be really pleased with elements of the performance on Tuesday night, we must absolutely know there is so much more to come from our team," he wrote in United's matchday programme.

"We must be ready to show that we can back up Tuesday's victory and begin to create the momentum to give ourselves something to build on after the international break."

The grim reality of United's present position was made clear by Nottingham Forest's 3-1 victory over Manchester City. That result means that Carrick's side will spend the international break in the relegation zone if they do not beat Villa.

Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.

Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with political parties after neither Eisenkot's bloc nor that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, following last week's election.

Eisenkot will now have 28 days to try to form a new administration, with a potential 14-day extension.

"Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," the former military chief wrote on X.

No political party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, meaning all governments have been coalitions.

Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.

Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.

That positions them as potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.

Herzog said that, after consulting all parties during the week, he would give Eisenkot the first chance to form a government.

A statement from the president's office said he had informed both Eisenkot and Netanyahu of the decision.

Following consultations with delegations from the incoming Knesset members, Eisenkot received 67 recommendations for the premiership and Netanyahu 46, the statement said.

The president has broad discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition and does not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.

The election results had implied three possible options for the formation of a government : a national unity administration involving both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.

Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but there has been speculation that an agreement could be reached.

He could also attempt to reach a deal with ultra-Orthodox parties, but that too would be difficult.

There is precedent for a unity government. In 2020, following three deadlocked elections, Netanyahu and his centrist rival Benny Gantz agreed a power-sharing deal in which the leadership rotated between the two.

During his consultations with the parties, Herzog had said that to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable government, he expected "factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled".

In the period 2019 to 2022, one of the most politically fractured in Israeli politics, there were five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate.

Tate's mum Tammy McDaid needs £3m for life-saving treatment for her child

The mum of a five-year-old boy with a rare form of dementia has to pay almost £3m for his life-saving treatment.

Tate McDaid, from Swansea, was diagnosed with Sanfilippo Syndrome , external - a form of dementia that just over 100 UK children have - when he was four .

In September, the first gene therapy to treat the condition in children was approved in the US.

His mum Tammy said she spent "months praying" for its approval but discovered the treatment is to set cost £2.95m per child, with it unclear how families outside the US can fund this.

Health officials from Wales were talking to those in the US to see what potential access pathways there were for Tate.

"I was excited when the treatment initially got approved but then reality hit hard the next day," Tammy said.

This was when she read the US price for the one-time treatment , external had been set at $3.95m.

Tammy contacted Ultragenyx, who developed the treatment, in the hope of understanding how families outside the US, who do not have health insurance there, will cover the costs.

"We understand what they are charging for American citizens, but they've got health insurance," she added.

"Not even just the UK, but everyone else in the world looking for this treatment."

Explaining how the US approved drug, FAYUVI, would work for families outside the US, Ultragenyx said: "There is not a single estimate we can provide for the total cost of care for an international patient, as those costs would depend on the patient's individual medical needs and the treating institution."

Sanfilippo Syndrome Type A, also known as Mucopolysaccharidosis type III (MPS III) , external , causes the gradual loss of abilities, such as walking and eating.

Because of its neurodegenerative nature, Sanfilippo Syndrome, is often called "childhood Alzheimer's" or "childhood dementia."

According to the Society for Mucopolysaccharide Diseases , external (MPS Society), a charity which helps children living with Sanfilippo Syndrome, about 140 children in the UK have the condition .

There is currently no cure for Sanfilippo Syndrome Type A, but the new drug could delay its onset, and allow Tate to remain active for longer.

It causes the gradual loss of abilities, such as walking and eating, and can progress more rapidly after the age of five, which is why Tammy said "it's really a battle of time" for her to raise enough money to get her son the treatment that is not available yet in the UK.

She said: "If a millionaire turned around tomorrow and gave us the money, we'd go to the US straight away."

With Tate turning six this month, Tammy does not believe time is on their side.

"Tate is already shown signs of cognitive decline," she added.

"The older he gets the less the treatment will work and the more ability he will lose in the process.

"I feel like we are at a turning point and I'm petrified."

Tammy said the new drug could help her son to keep his mobility for longer

Describing him as "the happiest little man" who is "blissfully unaware" of his problems, Tammy explained how important Tate's mobility is to him.

"He doesn't speak, he's never spoken. But his mobility is everything to him and that is why I'm fighting for it," she said.

Tammy began raising money before the new drug was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, and now has more than £160,000.

But this covers only about 5% of the total estimated cost of the treatment.

"Unfortunately, we're in a world where we need millions, not hundreds of thousands," she added.

"I'm just really hoping by some miracle the pharmaceutical company eventually come back to us and say they can do it for a little bit cheaper, but it's still going to be in the millions."

Tate's mum Tammy has raised more than £160,000 so far but hopes to reach £2.95m

Ultragenyx said: "We are pursuing a global regulatory strategy, and FDA approval is an important first step in our long-term goal of bringing this treatment option to families around the world.

"We also understand the urgency families affected by Sanfilippo syndrome Type A face in identifying treatment options and why some may consider travelling to the US to access gene therapy.

"We recommend families work with their child's healthcare provider to understand what potential access pathways may exist before assuming this is their only option."

Staff from the Noah's Ark Children's Hospital in Cardiff were discussing this with officials in the US on the family's behalf.

MN202611_1y8rdwlnm9v.t: Two Rwandan scientists have been elected as Fellows of The World Academy of Sciences (TWAS), joining an international network of researchers recognised for their contributions to scientific advancement and development. Prof. Eugénie Kayitesi, an expert in food science and nutrition, and Prof. Léon Mutesa, a specialist in human genetics were among 87 scientists elected as regular fellows during the academy's latest membership selection, announced on November 5. ALSO READ: Ex-minister Romain Murenzi earns top US science honour Their election takes effect on January 1, 2027. Four Rwandan scientists are now TWAS fellows. Prof. Romain Murenzi, a physicist and education minister, became a TWAS Fellow in 2005. Prof Agnès Binagwaho, a pediatrician and former health minister, became a TWAS Fellow in 2021. The recognition highlights Rwanda's growing contribution to international scientific research, particularly in areas relevant to the country's development, including food security, nutrition and medical research. Who are the newly elected fellows? Kayitesi is an Associate Professor in the Department of Consumer and Food Sciences at the University of Pretoria in South Africa. Her research focuses on food science and technology, particularly food chemistry, biochemistry and food processing. ALSO READ: Rwandan educator gets award from US university She specialises in improving the use of underutilised indigenous African crops to address food insecurity and malnutrition by transforming them into nutritious food products that can offer alternatives to expensive imported staples. She has published more than 100 research papers and book chapters and received several recognitions, including the 2023 OWSD-Elsevier Foundation Award and the 2022 Rwanda Women in Science Award. She is also a member of the African Academy of Sciences and the Pan-African Scientific Research Council. Speaking to The New Times on Sunday, Kayitesi described her election in the Agriculture, Nutrition and Food Systems Sciences category as an important personal milestone, particularly given that her academic journey began in Rwanda. She obtained a Bachelor of Science degree in Food Science and Technology from the University of Rwanda, formerly the Kigali Institute of Science and Technology (KIST). She is also an Honorary Visiting Professor at the UR College of Agriculture, Animal Sciences and Veterinary Medicine (UR-CAVM). My election validates a core mission anchored in my Rwandan heritage, proving that indigenous knowledge combined with rigorous science can solve Africa's most pressing food security and nutritional challenges, she said. ALSO READ: Africa not just a consumer but a contributor to global science, says Prof Murenzi Her research has focused on transforming underutilised African crops, including cereals, legumes and indigenous leafy vegetables, into climate-resilient, nutrient-rich food products. Through techniques such as fermentation, malting and infrared heating, her work seeks to improve nutrient absorption, reduce harmful substances in food and develop biofortified products that address protein-energy malnutrition and micronutrient deficiencies. Kayitesi said the Fellowship would also create opportunities to support emerging researchers through international research partnerships, mentorship and access to scientific networks. Membership in TWAS opens up international exchange programmes, postdoctoral opportunities, joint research grants and direct access to global networks such as the Organization for Women in Science for the Developing World (OWSD), she said. She added that she intends to mentor early-career Rwandan scientists and help them access international funding and research opportunities. She added that Rwanda needs to invest further in modern laboratory infrastructure, targeted grants for young researchers, particularly women in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM), and partnerships linking universities, government and businesses. Kayitesi also sees opportunities for her research to contribute directly to Rwanda's food security and economic development. She said processing locally available, drought-tolerant crops could extend their shelf life, reduce post-harvest losses and improve access to nutritious food throughout the year. By improving the availability of essential micronutrients such as iron and zinc, her research could also support efforts to address child malnutrition while creating markets for smallholder farmers and local food entrepreneurs. She is involved in the FEAT4AFRICA project, which seeks to promote sustainable development in African urban communities through innovations linking food, energy, water and health. Meanwhile, Mutesa is a Professor of Human Genetics and Director of the Centre for Human Genetics and Genomics at the University of Rwanda's College of Medicine and Health Sciences. He is recognised for his contribution to Rwanda's human genetics research capacity, including setting up the country's reference centre for human genetics in 2006, the only facility of its kind in East Africa. His research has examined how genetic and epigenetic changes, including those associated with trauma, may affect subsequent generations. He has particularly investigated the intergenerational effects of genocide-related trauma and post-traumatic stress disorder among women survivors of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and their offspring. Mutesa obtained his medical degree from the University of Rwanda in 2003 and a PhD from the University of Liège in Belgium in 2009. He later undertook postdoctoral research at the University of Erlangen in Germany. He previously served as Director General of the Medical Research Centre at the Rwanda Biomedical Centre (RBC). He is also a Fellow of the African Academy of Sciences and received the Human Genome Organisation (HUGO) African Prize in 2024. Where do other TWAS Fellows come from? According to The World Academy of Sciences, out of 87 regular Fellows, 58 are men and 29 are women, representing 33.3 per cent female membership. 77 come from countries in the Global South. Fifteen are from the 66 science- and technology-lagging countries (STLCs) identified by TWAS, including seven from Bangladesh and one each from Bolivia, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Nepal, Rwanda, Senegal and Zimbabwe. China leads in the number of newly elected Fellows with 13, followed by India with eight, Brazil with seven and South Africa with six. Nigeria, Malaysia and Saudi Arabia each have four. The Academy noted that Rwanda is among countries historically underrepresented in its membership. The latest elections bring TWAS's total membership to 1,510 Fellows across 10 scientific divisions, covering disciplines ranging from agriculture, nutrition and health sciences to engineering, physics, environmental sciences and social sciences.

Players and fans deserved this win - Glasner

The Oliver Glasner volcano could not contain the emotional lava of an impending first home Premier League victory any longer.

Nottingham Forest 's opening goal from Jair Cunha against Manchester City had drawn polite applause and a sedate thumbs-up from the Austrian manager.

Glasner was bubbling below the surface after Liam Delap's strike went in - dancing a merry jig in his technical area and hoisting his fists in the air.

When Delap rattled in Forest's third goal there was an eruption of joy from the 52-year-old.

Glasner sprinted down the touchline (well, as best a man in his early fifties can sprint) to join Forest's players as they mobbed the striker.

"One of my best running stats, I guess," Glasner joked to BBC Match of the Day after Forest's 3-1 win over City.

"I will be fatigued tomorrow but I can be because it's the international break so I can have a rest."

Forest's victory was their first in the league at the City Ground this season as Glasner's philosophy finally translated into that most precious of football commodities: goals.

Perhaps he was on to something when he said his side cannot survive on "flower power" , choosing a left-field comparison of the Woodstock music festival in the 1960s.

Up to this Saturday it had been a tale of frustration.

Despite having the second-most shots in the Premier League this season (152), they had scored the fewest goals (six).

They also had the lowest shot conversion rate (4%) and biggest negative xG (-8.3).

It was telling that at full-time in this match they had scored more goals against City (three) than they had in their previous six home league games combined (two).

It was reflected in their lowly standing in the table.

Forest had the biggest negative difference between points (six) and expected points (15.49), and also the biggest positional difference based on that (19th versus third).

"I think we've had better performances in possession because today we rarely had the ball. Regarding the team spirit, the energy, I think it was our best game," Glasner said.

"The way we play football I think we've had many better games but how we defended, how passionately we defended, how tactically smart we defended, it was one of our better games."

Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy said the result was a "huge moment in the season" for Forest.

"Glasner's actually been unlucky in the first part of his Forest tenure in terms of points they've got with the performances they've had," Murphy said.

"So that's a huge deal for him and the club."

Delap spent 10 years in City's academy before leaving for Ipswich in 2019.

His prolific form at Portman Road paved the way for a move to Chelsea , but he struggled to make an impact in west London and his career hit the buffers.

After managing just one goal in his first eight outings at the City Ground there were fears of regression, but he offered a timely reminder of the ability which persuaded Forest to shell out £50m for him with an electric display.

With his chest puffed out, Delap took the game to City's defence, driving at them with aggression, physicality and a determination to impose himself.

"When you come in with a price tag on your back everybody believes 'if you pay so much, he has to score all the goals'," Glasner added.

"He had one great season at Ipswich then lost a lot of confidence at Chelsea , so now he's getting better and better into rhythm."

It was the first time Delap has had two shots on target in a league match this season.

He scored with two of his three attempts against City (a 67% conversion), having scored just one goal from 24 shots in his first eight games (a 4% conversion).

"As a striker it's the most important thing [to score goals]," Delap added.

"The only thing you're judged on. You can play well and not score - really nice to score. Got to keep performing and improving but today I'm happy."

Murphy said Delap, son of former Derby, Southampton and Stoke defender Rory, is going to be a "really big player" for Forest this season.

"I think in recent weeks watching him play, he's looked fit, he's looked strong, he's got himself in good positions, and today he got the rewards of some goals to add to the performance," Murphy said.

"Like any striker, he loves scoring goals, but his all-round performance was good. And if he can stay fit, his confidence grows bit by bit each week."

New Zealand election 'too close to call' - so who's won?

New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather.

"It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread."

"Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits.

"I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confesses. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explains, declining to chat further.

"Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.

But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.

More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.

Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions.

A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.

Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate.

But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party – the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.

The Opportunity Party says it is willing to work with either of the major parties

"You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good," the party's ecstatic leader Quilae Wong told Kiwis on election night. "I personally came into this because I was frustrated at the slow pace of change."

It will likely be weeks before we know exactly who will make up the governing coalition and what deals have been made to form it.

But this is only the first of many challenges facing whoever is the next prime minister of a country at a crossroads.

New Zealand hasn't always felt like this.

For a long time, the country was viewed as a land of milk and honey – literally – for those who worked hard, with its people ranking amongst the most positive in the world.

A satisfying career, access to quality healthcare, and a close network of family and friends – which research suggests are the three most important building blocks of a happy life – were all there for the taking, University of Auckland Prof Robert MacCulloch says.

"The lifestyle was good," the world-leader in the study of happiness economics tells the BBC. "You weren't the highest paid, but you could get by nicely."

Many young people like Michael Dawson (left) feel like they can't get ahead

Many who spoke to the BBC said the country's decline accelerated into a dive during the Covid pandemic.

Unemployment is now at an 11-year high and rising. For Kiwis aged under 24, things haven't been this bad in three decades: jobs are so scarce that one in three either cannot get enough work or have none at all.

Michael Dawson says he did everything he thought he was supposed to: finished school, studied a trade and obtained a qualification, and has applied for dozens of jobs.

But it's been a year now and the job market is so dire he hasn't had a single interview.

"It has sucked. A lot... I'm somewhat cynical with the way I think [about the future] now," the 20-year-old says.

Zainab Ali, chief executive of support service Youth Inspire, has never seen demand so high, with waitlists for its employment aid workshops stretching into the hundreds.

The young people who do make it through their doors on the outskirts of Wellington are disheartened.

"The things we used to hear from everyone's grumpy uncle around the Christmas table sometimes, our young people are now starting to give us that same feedback: like, 'What's the point?'"

Sam says he's flirted with a move to Australia

Meanwhile, household electricity bills have jumped drastically, partly driven by global supply shocks. New Zealand remains one of the least affordable places on Earth to rent or buy a home. High inflation means every dollar is having to stretch further.

The island nation produces enough food to feed its population eight times over, but about a quarter of adults are skipping meals because the price of groceries – set by a supermarket duopoly – is among the highest in the developed world.

And the headlines are full of healthcare crises: long waiting lists, chronic understaffing, crumbling health infrastructure and climbing costs for patients. Few stories have captured the state of the system like the death of a man who collapsed in an emergency department toilet after a nine-hour wait in July.

"There's a segment of the population that are facing real material hardship... and then there's another segment of New Zealanders that are quite anxious that they could be next," political scientist Luke Oldfield, from Victoria University of Wellington, says.

Increasingly polarised public debate – around topics like Māori rights and the Treaty of Waitangi, healthcare for LGBT+ people and immigration – have added to the mental load for many in those communities.

"There's been a few groups feeling like they're being used as a political football," Dr Lara Greaves, who studies Indigenous politics, says.

This perfect storm is driving about 180 people to leave the country every day – a record-breaking exodus that is dividing families, shrinking communities and draining talent pools.

Siblings Sam and Emily tell the BBC that they love New Zealand but find it hard to keep finding reasons to stay. Their friends are leaving en masse and even their parents have considered moving to Australia.

"It's not just that you're being rewarded for going to Australia, it's that you're kind of actively being punished for staying here," Sam says.

Stu thinks New Zealand is on its way back up

There are still large parts of the country that feel differently, though.

At the nation's largest livestock saleyard in the town of Feilding, where farmers from all over the island have gathered, Stu Morton says the last year was the best he's had in his 30-year career.

The agriculture industry - which makes up about 3% of New Zealand's GDP - was struggling under the previous Labour government's emissions reductions scheme, he adds, but has turned a corner under the National Party.

He believes the rest of the economy will follow suit.

"We've been through those times where you're questioning 'Where's the future?'

"What helps is having a stable government... [and] it comes down to a positive attitude - appreciating that what you've got is actually okay."

Many of these issues affecting New Zealand are global trends - and it's undeniable that Kiwis' standard of living is better than many others.

But these issues are having a corrosive impact on its national identity.

"It leads to a crisis of confidence about what New Zealand is and where it's going," Helen Clark, who was prime minister from 1999 to 2008, tells the BBC.

Her foundation surveys New Zealanders every year about social cohesion, and its most recent report found Kiwis - in particular young people - feel far more isolated than they did a generation ago, attitudes towards multiculturalism are souring and the population is becoming less hopeful.

Faith in institutions and leaders has taken an alarming turn: only two out of five New Zealanders trust the government to do the right thing, while less than half of the country trusts the courts.

"There's a feeling that, really, there's no-one who cares," Clark says.

National Party leader Christopher Luxon is seeking a second term

The transformation former Labour prime minister Jacinda Ardern promised on issues like healthcare and housing when she was elected in 2017 never eventuated. Many other achievements - for example world leading smoking reforms, emissions reduction policies or Māori language initiatives - have been wound back by her successors.

Her legacy is dominated by polarising Covid decisions, as is Chris Hipkins', who was health minister before his eight months in the top job after Ardern's resignation .

The National Party came to power in 2023 promising to "get our country back on track" and rebuild the economy.

"You'd have to say they've had very limited success," political commentator Grant Duncan says. "And the Luxon government can only blame the previous government for so long."

National delivered the education overhaul it pledged, but the biggest moment of their tenure was the massive hikoi – protest march – led by Māori over their coalition partner's unpopular bill to redefine the Treaty of Waitangi. And then came the two leadership challenges Christopher Luxon fought off in the past six months.

Former PM Chris Hipkins has been leader of New Zealand's centre-left Labour Party since January 2023

There's a sense Labour had too much ambition, much of it costly and unfulfilled, while National doesn't have enough, having spent much of its time and effort wrangling their own flank.

Both governments say their plans for the country were stymied by crises out of their control – such as Covid, the Iran war and US trade antagonism.

But Duncan says that's not cutting it with voters. He's never seen the country quite like this before: "Neither of the parties has been able to field a really strong, inspiring leader. Both of them have a track record of disappointing results."

No matter who ends up taking the top job, Sam says he's not convinced much will change.

"It does just feel stale... a lot of the population probably feels like we could do a bit better," he says. With a wry smile, he adds: "I don't think it helps that they're two white guys named Chris."

Enzo Maresca left the City Ground on Saturday evening with chants of "can we play you every week?" ringing in his ears - and the Italian's dream start as Manchester City manager is rapidly turning into a nightmare.

Amid a sea of noise from the home faithful on the banks of the River Trent, the delirious Forest supporters witnessed their side produce a thrilling performance as City sunk to a third straight Premier League loss.

Maresca's leaky backline continues to make defensive blunders and once Josko Gvardiol gave the ball away for Jair Cunha to open the scoring in the sixth minute, City were on the back foot.

With Arsenal edging past Hull earlier in the day and keeping another clean sheet, City head into the international break searching for answers after a 3-1 loss and six points behind the champions.

Maresca said: "The first half we didn't match [Forest's] intensity or win duels or second balls. The first thing required in these games is intensity.

"We tried to react at 2-0 but it's too late. We scored one, probably could have scored more but in transition we concede one more. No panic. We need to understand but no panic."

Asked why the intensity was low, Maresca replied: "I need to analyse that."

The situation already looks bleak for City, but what does history show?

Should Brighton fail to beat Brentford on Sunday, Arsenal would be just the fourth side in Premier League history to have a six-point lead after 10 games, while only two teams have been so far behind as City at this stage and gone on to win the title.

One of those was Manchester United in 2002-03. The other? City themselves in 2013-14 under Manuel Pellegrini.

But Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton have the opportunity to leap up to second place and five points behind the Gunners should they beat Brentford .

There is another factor which looms large over City's campaign.

The club have lodged an appeal after being found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules .

That process is ongoing - and it is not yet known what potential sanctions City could face.

But - even if any possible punishment does not affect this season - their title hopes are looking slimmer by the match.

Delightful Delap and outfought Anderson - Forest v Man City player ratings

Has Anderson lived up to the hype after Man City move?

With his hands tucked inside his trouser pockets and his head bowed, a forlorn-looking Maresca paced the touchline towards the end of the match.

The City boss said during the week he was still getting to know his players, but performances like the one against Forest will provide some clarity as to who he can, and cannot, trust.

After starting the season with seven straight wins, City have hit real trouble with defeats against Aston Villa , Brighton and now a pumped-up Forest.

Their problems at the back are not helping as it was another game where individual errors cost them dearly - and former striker Liam Delap took full advantage of the lapses in concentration with two goals.

Gvardiol was at fault for the first, Iliman Ndiaye and Elliot Anderson got in a muddle for the second, while Matheus Nunes did not put a challenge in for the third.

"Before the game all the talk was about individual errors," former Forest winger Steve Stone told BBC Radio 5 Live. "Apart from the first goal, this hasn't been about that - the line is disjointed.

"The full-backs were very wide. If the ball turns over quickly and you pass it with your first pass you can be right through them. They have been exposed today.

"Oliver Glasner's team have played through them every time."

It was a miserable return to the City Ground for Anderson since his £116m move to City in the summer and the midfield dynamic alongside Enzo Fernandez does not seem to be working.

The Argentine should have scored with a headed chance from close range but spent much of the game complaining in referee Sam Barrott's ear - City team-mates and supporters may be expecting more from their club record signing.

The former Chelsea player scored in the midweek Champions League win at RB Leipzig, but that is his only goal or assist in his past nine games.

Maresca needs to work out how to get the best out of Fernandez during the international break.

Stone added: "I came here tonight thinking City would win, I thought they had chances. This is a real hammer blow to them, there is something not right about the back four at the minute.

"I have never seen a City team give the ball away so much in the middle of the park."

Rayan Cherki's stunning strike gave City hope but they could not turn it around and the numbers following the result make for grim:

City have lost three consecutive Premier League games for the first time since a run of four in November-December 2024

They have become the second team in English top-flight history - after Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05 - to win their first seven games of a season and then lose their next three

This was their first league defeat by two or more goals against a side starting the day in the relegation zone since November 2008 (a 2-0 loss to Bolton Wanderers).

Maresca was forced to chop and change his defence again, withdrawing both Gvardiol and Marc Guehi at half-time because of injuries, according to the manager.

It meant Nunes came in at right-back, with Abdukodir Khusanov moving inside, and Nico O'Reilly playing down the left.

Former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy told BBC Sport: "I thought City's performance was poor in terms of mentality.

"To make so make so many mistakes when you go anywhere in the Premier League, but especially to a team who are fighting for the lives, and you know they're going to come after you.

"They were sloppy with the ball, not winning duels. I would even probably go as far as saying there was probably a bit of arrogance at the start of the game from them.

"I think that there are now some big questions to ask the manager about how he gets them back on track. I think with the talent they have got, it is not going to be a big problem.

"But I think defensively, maybe sticking to the same backline for a little while is the way forward."

MWANZA, Tanzania — On the shores of Lake Victoria, a wedding that brought together some of East Africa’s most prominent political families unfolded with the colour, ceremony and intimacy of a major family occasion.

Charlene Ruto, daughter of Kenyan President William Ruto and First Lady Rachel Ruto, married Tanzanian entrepreneur and businessman Isaya Yunge on Friday, November 6, 2026, in an elaborate white wedding at Malaika Beach Hotel and Resort in Mwanza.

The ceremony took place in the groom’s home region and brought together family members, political leaders, business figures and friends from across East Africa.

For the Ruto family, the wedding marked the culmination of months of preparations that began with a traditional Kalenjin Koito ceremony in August.

The engagement and farewell ceremony was held at the Ruto family’s Intonna Heritage Farm in Kilgoris, Narok County, Kenya.

The wedding celebrations then moved through several family occasions before arriving in Mwanza.

On November 3, Charlene was celebrated at a bridal shower in Kenya, held around a white-and-purple theme. Rachel Ruto also hosted a “Mother’s Blessing” ceremony for her daughter.

The occasion carried a strong family and Christian symbolism. Charlene received gifts including a Bible, a framed verse from Proverbs 31, roses, suitcases and slippers.

By the time she arrived in Mwanza, the celebrations had taken on a distinctly Tanzanian character.

Charlene received a colourful traditional welcome, with dancers and luxury vehicles accompanying her arrival.

The main ceremony was held outdoors and was presided over by the Africa Inland Church in Tanzania.

The setting was designed around the natural beauty of Lake Victoria.

White floral arches framed the ceremony. A mirrored aisle, lined with white flowers, led towards the altar. White drapes and tents surrounded the seating area, creating an elegant setting against the lake.

The most emotional moment came when President Ruto and Rachel Ruto walked their daughter down the aisle.

The images quickly became among the most widely shared moments from the wedding, showing the Kenyan president and his wife accompanying their daughter through one of the most important moments of her life.

Charlene and Yunge exchanged vows and rings before joining their families for photographs.

The bride wore an elaborate white gown decorated with three-dimensional floral embellishments across the bodice and skirt.

The structured dress was completed by a long cathedral-style veil and a decorative hair accessory. She carried a bouquet featuring white and red roses, or flowers in similar shades.

For portraits and other moments, she later appeared in a second white outfit, a midi dress with cap sleeves and a lace-trimmed veil.

Gold and pearl earrings and other accessories completed her bridal looks.

Yunge wore a formal cream-coloured or classic white suit, although reports differed slightly on details such as the tie.

Charlene’s sisters, including Stephanie, June, Nadia and Cullie, formed part of the bridal party.

They wore elegant red and burgundy off-the-shoulder gowns and carried white rose bouquets.

Other members of the Ruto family, including siblings Nick, George, June and Nadia, were also present.

The bridal party reflected the family-centred character of the occasion. Some reports noted that there was little emphasis on a conventional group of groomsmen.

Among the distinguished guests was Rwanda’s First Lady, Mrs Jeannette Kagame.

Her presence gave the wedding another regional dimension.

She was photographed with members of the Ruto family, including President Ruto and Rachel Ruto, and participated in the celebrations.

She also delivered a special message on behalf of her husband, Rwanda’s President Paul Kagame.

Her message was brief but personal, focusing not on politics but on the foundations of a lasting marriage.

“I’m bringing greetings from my husband, the President of Rwanda.”

Turning to the newlyweds, she read the message prepared in Swahili language:

“Today, you have become husband and wife. It is a very happy day.”

She then offered the couple one piece of advice.

“Love each other through actions, not just through words.”

“Listen to each other, respect each other, and forgive each other.”

She ended with a blessing for the new family they were beginning together.

“Build your home with love, peace and faith. May God bless you greatly. Congratulations.”

The remarks were delivered in a formal setting, attracted applause from attendees, as she stood with a microphone against a floral backdrop.

Videos of the speech, showing her in a dark blue or purple dress and occasionally consulting her notes or phone, circulated widely on Rwandan social media.

Her appearance quickly became one of the most discussed elements of the wedding among Rwandan audiences.

The message also carried a regional significance.

Rwanda, Kenya and Tanzania are members of the East African Community, and the wedding brought together families connected to three countries at a time when regional integration remains an important political and economic project.

Yet Jeannette Kagame’s message remained firmly focused on the couple.

Instead, she spoke about love, respect, forgiveness, peace and faith.

Her advice reflected the intimate nature of the occasion and the role she had been invited to play as a distinguished guest of the family.

President Ruto and Rachel Ruto also attracted considerable attention with their outfits.

Ruto wore a distinctive burgundy and red patterned jacket over a white shirt, complemented by a bow tie, hat and cane.

Rachel wore a long floral maroon and pink dress with a wide-brimmed matching hat.

The couple’s presence added another layer to an occasion that was already attracting considerable attention across East Africa.

The guest list included senior Kenyan political figures.

National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula attended, as did Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi and his spouse.

Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen, Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale and several members of Parliament and governors were also present.

Comedian Eddie Butita was also among the guests.

Uganda was represented by Rt Hon Rukia Nakadama, who attended on behalf of President Yoweri Museveni.

Nakadama presented the newlyweds with a gift of USD20,000.

Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan was not prominently reported among those attending the ceremony.

There were also reports of guests arriving by private jet and of tight security around the event.

After the wedding, President Ruto shared an emotional public message reflecting on his daughter’s journey into marriage.

He praised Charlene’s growth and welcomed Yunge into the family.

His advice centred on the qualities he said would help the couple build a lasting marriage: friendship, patience, kindness and forgiveness.

He also offered prayers and blessings for the couple, including wishes for good health, prosperity and children.

The message gave a more personal dimension to a wedding that had otherwise been dominated by images of political leaders, elaborate clothing and a spectacular lakeside setting.

For Ruto, the occasion was not simply the marriage of a daughter.

It was also the moment when a daughter he had watched grow up formally began a new family of her own.

The Mwanza wedding generated extensive coverage in Kenya, Tanzania and Rwanda, with photographs and videos spreading rapidly across social media.

Images of Charlene walking down the mirrored aisle with her parents were among the most circulated.

So were photographs of the bride and groom, the bridal party, the Ruto family and Jeannette Kagame.

In Rwanda, particular attention focused on the First Lady’s attendance and her message to the couple.

Clips posted on X, Facebook and other platforms attracted thousands of views and reactions, with much of the conversation centred on the glamour of the wedding, the families involved and the cross-border nature of the celebration.

The event did not become a major global news story in the way that some royal or celebrity weddings do.

It brought together political and business networks from across East Africa while remaining, at its heart, a family celebration.

The wedding also demonstrated how private family occasions involving the region’s political elite can become informal spaces for relationship-building.

There were no formal policy announcements in Mwanza.

Instead, the message came through presence.

Kenya’s president and his family hosted a wedding in Tanzania. Rwanda’s First Lady travelled to join the celebration and delivered greetings from President Kagame. Uganda sent a senior representative and a substantial gift.

The result was a gathering that blended traditional Kalenjin customs, Tanzanian hospitality, Christian ceremony and the social networks of East Africa’s political establishment.

Against the backdrop of Lake Victoria, Charlene Ruto and Isaya Yunge began their marriage surrounded not only by family and friends, but by a region whose political, economic and personal ties increasingly cross national borders.

It was not pretty, but Martin Odegaard's goal was enough to secure the 1-0 win that ensured Arsenal go into the international break as the Premier League leaders.

It was Arsenal's 34th 1-0 win under Mikel Arteta, to equal their best start to a Premier League season under the Spaniard of 27 points earned after 10 games in 2022-23.

No team has enjoyed more 1-0 wins since Arteta was appointed back in 2019, with the Gunners winning their past 10 home games in all competitions, keeping eight clean sheets in that time.

Odegaard's goal though, bundled home from close range, may well have been a relief to those at Pro Ref, too.

A controversial video assistant referee (VAR) decision, which denied the Gunners a first-half penalty, threatened to be the story as a largely uneventful game drifted by.

When referee Farai Hallam was sent to the pitchside monitor for a VAR review for a shirt pull by Nobel Mendy on Kai Havertz, surely everyone inside the Emirates was expecting a penalty.

The irony would not be lost on Liverpool fans, who were denied a VAR penalty for a shirt pull last weekend when Arsenal 's Jurrien Timber tugged back Alexander Isak.

Unlike Isak, Havertz made sure everyone - including VAR Michael Oliver, was aware that a defender had hold of his shirt.

Indeed, the cheers had already begun when Hallam started to describe the foul to the crowd - but Gunners supporters were stopped in their tracks. The referee pivoted to an offside against Havertz, and play restarted with a free-kick to Hull .

Had Arsenal not mustered that 72nd-minute winner from their captain, much of the attention would, once again, have been on VAR.

Tottenham set to complain to Pro Ref - but should Bogle have seen red?

Odegaard hits winner as Arsenal beat Hull to extend lead at top

Mikel Arteta post-match interview - Arsenal v Hull

If Arsenal had dropped points, it wouldn't have been the first time this weekend that a match would have been dominated by discussions about the video officials.

On Friday, Coventry City were denied what appeared to be a clear penalty against Everton for a hair pull by James Tarkowski on Caleb Yirenkyi. Then in the second half, when Thierno Barry scored to put the Toffees 2-1 up and the ball appeared to come off his hand.

The controversy continued in Saturday's early kick-off between Leeds and Tottenham. First, Leeds wanted a penalty for handball by Mateus Fernandes, though replays did show the ball hit the Spurs player's shoulder.

Then came the potential red card for a challenge by Jayden Bogle on Mathys Tel, which has split opinion. The VAR, Tony Harrington, eventually decided after a four-minute VAR check that the foul did not have enough force.

That Tel was forced off injured, and referee John Brooks did not even show a yellow card on the field, only added to the frustration for Tottenham .

So on to the Emirates, and again the debate was around VAR.

It's a situation few would question. After all, an offside player winning a penalty surely goes against the very logic of the law?

If an offside player is running to the ball and is fouled before they attempt to play the ball or challenge an opponent, then the foul is considered to come before the offside offence.

The law seeks to prevent situations whereby defenders have carte blanche to foul attackers, just because the opponent is offside.

Former Premier League assistant referee Darren Cann told BBC Match of the Day: “The foul should have taken precedence over the offside and it should have been a penalty. The law is very ambiguous though.”

But is a complex area of law and is very much open to interpretation.

In February 2019, the season before VAR came in, an offside Harry Kane was awarded a late penalty in a north London derby after being dragged down by Shkodran Mustafi.

Two years ago, Newcastle were awarded a spot-kick against Bournemouth through a VAR intervention when Adam Smith tugged back an offside Fabian Schar.

Yet last December, after being awarded a penalty against Leeds , Brentford 's Dango Ouattara was ruled to be offside and the spot-kick ruled out through VAR.

So which interpretation is correct? Kane and Schar, or Havertz and Ouattara?

Ouattara was somewhat different, as he appeared to be engaging with Gabriel Gudmundsson as the ball was played.

The Havertz example is more like the one involving Schar, who was running forward when his shirt was tugged back.

But there is an additional consideration, and this is where Oliver's thinking will lie.

Officials are asked to consider the likelihood of the attacker becoming involved in the play from a second phase. Let's say the ball could be first played by a team-mate, which then makes them onside. Then they are not purely benefitting from being offside.

In the case of Schar and Kane, they could have benefitted from that second phase.

Havertz was the only attacker who had any chance of being involved in the play, so the VAR determined offside was the fair outcome.

At least tonight most of the talk will be about another victory for Arsenal - and not VAR.

Goal caps eye-catching Odegaard display - player ratings for Arsenal v Hull

Another game, another win but still Arsenal are looking for their attack to spark into life.

At the end of the day results matter but Arsenal , despite being top, are the lowest scorers of the teams in the top four.

They have the best defence in the league and arguably Europe but goals are also seeming hard to come by at the other end.

Arsenal have not scored more than twice in the league since the opening day of the season, when they put three past Coventry .

Arteta's side are missing talisman Bukayo Saka, who is out with a quadricep injury, and has a unique partnership with Ben White and Martin Odegaard on the right.

On the left Christos Tzolis started the season well but, after a hamstring injury while playing for Greece, the 24-year-old has not looked the same threat.

The same can be said for Kai Havertz too.

The 27-year-old picked up a hamstring injury playing for Germany and, even though he scored the winner against Liverpool , his performances have not reached the same level.

Viktor Gyokeres is firmly second choice this season and Arteta is still working out how to get the best out of the maverick Eberechi Eze, while Noni Madueke is working to fill the gap left by Saka.

Arteta was asked about the number of single-goal wins this season and what he can do to improve that.

"To be more efficient," was the answer the Gunners boss gave. "We are one against one against the keeper. That's happened twice today.

"There is a penalty there, there is another situation inside the box where the ball is bouncing. So many shots that have been deflected, blocked. We need to find ways to be more efficient, sometimes even more pragmatic.

"Sometimes my feeling is that we are trying to score a perfect goal against these low blocks. We need to be much more chaotic than that, and that's it. And open, I think, score much earlier because obviously that's going to change the course of the game."

Even if the Gunners could be more free-flowing going forward, they have started the season in a formidable way - winning nine of their 10 league games.

And if they manage to keep up that rate of winning, the Gunners will likely defend their Premier League crown and win back-to-back titles for the first time in 100 years.

Level on points at the top of the Women's Super League, there was little to separate Chelsea and Manchester City in the title race as they kicked off their respective matches at the same time on Saturday.

At that stage, Chelsea were edging the reigning champions thanks to a comfortably better goal difference, built up via a ruthlessness in attack and a solid defence.

However, by full-time, the tables had turned with Sonia Bompastor's side forced to settle for a point in a 1-1 draw against Everton, despite dominating at Stamford Bridge.

While Chelsea struggled to put their chances away, Khadija Shaw - a summer transfer target for the Blues - was running riot at Joie Stadium, and her hat-trick inspired Manchester City to an emphatic 5-0 victory against West Ham, trimming the goal difference gap in the process.

The win moves City two points clear of Chelsea at the top, one week before the sides meet in a potential title decider.

Yet Shaw, who has scored 12 goals in nine league appearances this season and is two away from equalling Vivianne Miedema's all-time WSL record of 97 goals, is not getting carried away.

"There's a lot of games to play, a lot of twists and turns," she told Sky Sports.

"One game at a time. We've got Champions League midweek and then we go again. We have to focus on the task ahead and not get too complacent."

Shaw hat-trick helps Man City back to top of table

Bronze scores own goal as Chelsea held by Everton

Chelsea surrender top spot after home draw with Everton

With Everton ranked eighth and West Ham placed 10th at the start of the day, both games - on paper - looked favourable for the league's top two sides.

At Stamford Bridge, the Toffees did not have a shot on target and had just three touches in their opponent's box, while Chelsea had 20 shots, an expected goals total of 2.14 and 55 touches in the Everton penalty area - to no avail.

At the other end, Lucy Bronze's unfortunate own goal ultimately cost them three points.

"We weren't quite on the same page today but I cannot fault anyone's effort," Chelsea captain Erin Cuthbert said.

"It's just one of those days where we're not at the races and we can't have too many of those if we want to be in a title race."

Bompastor's side resorted to hopeful crosses and shots from range, while they lacked creativity against a resilient Everton side.

The Blues were not helped by Lauren James' absence, the playmaker ruled out for at least five games after sustaining a hamstring injury in last weekend's 6-0 victory over Charlton.

Chelsea and Manchester City had the same number of shots on Saturday

In Manchester, City waited patiently for an opener against West Ham and once they got it - thanks to Shaw's composed finish - the floodgates opened.

Shaw and Lauren Hemp - despite both missing out on the 26-player Fifpro Women's World XI shortlist - are an unstoppable duo in City's attack, with City's first goal the fifth time they have combined in the WSL this season.

"It's hard to explain. We just click. It's a connection we've built over time," Hemp told BBC Radio 5 Live. "It's not always perfect, but with the standards we set for each other, naturally it's going to come."

Already a two-time Golden Boot winner, Shaw appears to be in the form of her life. Her 12 goals this season account for 44% of City's WSL strikes - but goals from Aoba Fujino and Iman Beney against West Ham suggest Jeglertz still has other options.

"Our depth is going to be crucial. We can put players on that can bring us to the next level," the City boss told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"We are going to need all players. Five games in two weeks. Some players are starting, some are finishing, some are supporting from the side.

"We are all very important for success and this showed in this game."

Shaw hat-trick gives five-star Man City dominant win over West Ham

Chelsea will not have to wait long for a chance to overhaul City as victory against the champions next Saturday would put them back in top spot.

"We need to move on quickly," Bompastor said. "This group has a lot of experience with that and we will go into the next game really prepared.

"When we are doing well, it's good not to go too high - when it doesn't work, it's good not to get too low."

City have won their past two games against Chelsea - including last season's FA Cup semi-final - but the club know from past experience that it is far too early in the season to be complacent.

In the 2023-24 campaign, City were three points clear at the WSL summit with just two games left to play, but they ended up losing the title on goal difference to Chelsea on the final day of the season.

"At the moment, I don't care about it so much," Jeglertz said when asked about Chelsea dropping points.

"Of course I don't want them to win, but we also know that to win this league, we have to battle the whole way.

"If we win all our games, we'll be fine but if we struggle, then of course it doesn't matter what other teams do."

The US has announced a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear programme.

The State Department's Rewards for Justice is also offering to potentially relocate the person who provides such details.

President Donald Trump claimed last year that Iran's nuclear facilities had been "completely and totally obliterated " following a bombing campaign by the US and Israel.

Iran insists its nuclear programme is peaceful and that it has no intention of developing a nuclear weapon.

Meanwhile, the US military says it is setting up a task force to enhance Washington's efforts to restrict Iran's movement of weapons and sanctioned material across its borders.

The US military's Central Command (Centcom) said Task Force Iron Gate would operate from Tampa, Florida, and would work with other US government agencies.

As well as the movement of weapons, it will also focus on dual-use and illegal revenue streams.

Centcom estimates that its naval blockade of Iran's ports has prevented the country from exporting more than $25bn in crude oil.

Major construction ongoing near Iran missile bases, satellite images suggest

A US State Department statement about its multi-million dollar reward said it was offering the money for information about the Iranian programme, including "facilities, equipment and associated personnel".

It said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA [the International Atomic Energy Agency] on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like [nuclear] centrifuges".

Centrifuges are needed to produce enriched uranium, which can be used to make reactor fuel for civilian use but also for nuclear weapons if enriched to around 90% purity or higher.

There had been mounting speculation that the US might resume significant strikes in Iran after the midterm elections, though Trump told reporters, prior to the polls, that he was in "no rush" to do so.

In an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms, the president also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme.

This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump said.

The president has repeatedly threatened to bomb the suspected underground site on previous occasions.

However, both Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have said public opposition to the war on Iran fuelled heavy losses for their Republican Party in this week's midterm elections, which has led to speculation the White House may no longer seek an escalation in the conflict.

On Friday, Trump insisted that Iran was keen to end the eight-month conflict with the US, stressing the damage to Tehran's economy and military.

"We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said.

Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.

Iranian negotiators had discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Roberto De Zerbi post-match interview - Leeds v Spurs

Tottenham are set to submit a formal complaint about the decision not to send off Jayden Bogle for his challenge on Mathys Tel during the defeat by Leeds .

Bogle, 26, escaped any punishment despite catching Spurs forward Tel on the back of the ankle with his studs in the first half of Saturday's game.

It is understood Tottenham believe Bogle should have been sent off and will write to refereeing body Pro Ref to seek an explanation as to why the incident did not result in a dismissal.

The challenge was reviewed thoroughly by the Video Assistant Referee (VAR), but referee John Brooks was not sent to the pitch-side monitor, meaning Bogle escaped any punishment.

Former Premier League assistant referee Darren Cann said the Leeds defender was "fortunate" not to be dismissed.

"Bogle's challenge meets the criteria for serious foul play as he endangers the safety of an opponent," Cann told BBC Sport. "He can consider himself lucky to still be on the pitch."

By the time play resumed, there were less than nine minutes of the first half remaining and Tottenham 's momentum - and composure - were fading quickly.

Roberto de Zerbi's side never appeared to recover from the incident and, after the break, were outworked and outplayed by the home side.

Nevertheless, the Italian - perhaps buoyed by his side's recent rise up the table - refused to pinpoint Spurs ' failings on the referee's decision.

"We deserved to lose the game in the second half and didn't play like we can," he told TNT Sports. "It's a journey for us because we can learn from this game.

"I am sorry for the performance in the second half - we didn't play like a top team. We didn't have the right character and physicality in the second half."

Okafor downs Tottenham to earn Leeds first win since September

Okafor the difference despite Van Hecke defiance - Leeds v Spurs ratings

Tottenham's defeat at Leeds was the first time they had lost a Premier League game since September

When the PA system at Elland Road confirmed there was a VAR check in progress, it seemed only a matter of time before Bogle would be shown a red card.

The Leeds defender was full-blooded in his pursuit of the ball from Tel and seemed certain to follow in the footsteps of Crystal Palace forward Jean-Philippe Mateta, who was sent off for a similar challenge against Spurs last weekend.

What was strange about the situation, though, was that at no point did Brooks make his way to the pitchside monitor to review the incident.

It meant the entire four-minute review was conducted solely by those in the VAR hub at Stockley Park.

"They've said no red card, and this will create debate," former Tottenham midfielder Michael Brown told BBC Radio 5 Live.

And because Brooks had not initially cautioned Bogle, the defender escaped the incident without any punishment.

"I have big confidence in the referee. Nothing changes if he goes to the monitor," said De Zerbi. "If they didn't take the right decision I don't know. We have to keep the eyes on the performance where can improve."

Early in the second half, Tottenham 's frustration - seemingly stemming from the decision not to dismiss Bogle - came to a head when defender Pedro Porro and De Zerbi himself were booked simultaneously following a challenge by the Spanish defender.

De Zerbi described the decision to caution Porro as "incredible" after what had transpired during the first half.

"I was surprised on the yellow card for Pedro Porro because it was clear," the Italian told BBC Match of the Day. "The potential red card, I couldn't say.

"We have full confidence in the referee and VAR. I cannot say nothing more."

Bogle was certainly very lucky to escape even a booking.

The foul happened in strange circumstances. Bogle was positioning his body to challenge Tel with his right foot, and in trying to plant his left foot he stood on the ankle of the Spurs player.

At full speed it looked innocuous, which is probably why referee Brooks chose not to show a card after giving the foul.

Once the slow-motion replays were looked at it became apparent that the nature of the contact on Tel was very ugly, with the twist of the ankle.

It could easily have resulted in the VAR, Tony Harrington, sending Brooks to the pitchside monitor for an on-field review for a red card.

Harrington spent far too long looking at the replays, probably feeling he had more time while Tel received treatment. But longer reviews only tend to cause doubts about process.

Harrington eventually told Brooks: "I'm confirming the on-field decision of no red card. There's a lack of speed going into the challenge and he's stepping into the tackle. Confirming a reckless challenge."

A reckless challenge is a yellow card, but the VAR is unable to intervene and advise that Bogle should be booked.

Something else Harrington said is important - "stepping into the challenge".

It does not mean a player cannot be sent off, but this is far less likely to result in a VAR review for a red card because such challenges naturally come with less force.

How about comparisons with Mateta's VAR red card against Spurs last week?

There is an argument that Mateta, who was booked on-field, made less forceful contact on the ankle of Micky van de Ven. Yet it is the nature of the challenge that is crucially different.

Mateta made a lunging, stretching tackle with studs leading, the kind generally considered to come with a higher degree of force and potential danger to the opponent.

That said, and even though Bogle was not really making a challenge, the nature of the contact means many may feel there should have been a VAR review for a red card.
